CHUNGKING
Oct. 29th, 1988
PersonaL
Mr. S. I. Morgan,
Pan American Airways,
Now York, N. I.
Dear liz. Morgan,
Everything has been moving so rapidly the last week
or so I have juat about lost all track of time, In my letter of Oct.
19th I agein prediated the fall of Hanksow but I certainly bad no idea
it would fell so soon.
On the twenty first we received sone urgent messages
from the Minister who was in Hankow requesting us to immediately increase
our service to lankow and advising us confidentially that the city wea
personal messages over the commercial telegraph from government officials
I knew asicing me to arrange charter trips for them so it was evident the
situation in Hankow was getting tense.
It was impossible to increase our schedules with the
flying boats as they were practically flying every day anyway so the
only thing we could do would be to use the DC-tros at night. We could go
into Hankow at night safely because the military field is equipped fot
night flying and the country all around is flat, but night flying into
Chungking is impossible except on very rare occasions.
We therefore would
have to fly from Hankow to Chengtu.
We therefore agreed to fly from
Chungking to Hankow, Leaving so as to arrive in Henkow soon after dark and
then fly to Chengtu and back to lankow arriving just before day light and
then make a second flight out of Honkow for Chungking•
He decided to drop
the steward and take fifteen passengers. This was a rather anbitious
schedule and would require every break in order to accomplish it. We only
had two pilots with night flying experience who could do it, Sharp and
Leonard and Sherp was in Hongkong. Aiso there were no night landing
facilities at Chengtu, so
we would have to arrange for them. We therefore
sent Leonard to Hongkong
that afternoon, he was scheduled to go anyway, with
instructions to return that night with Sharp. I sent Sharp a messege to
get a floodlight that would work from a storage battery, and be prepared to
return to Chungking with Leonard. They both arrived about nine o'clock on
the morning of the 22nd. I discussed the situation with them and they
thought it could be done. Leonard who had been flying nearly sil night
went up to where I live and went to bed. He sent Nich to Chengtu with the
flood 1ight and a lot of lanterns to arrange for the 1ighte and to have gos
and o11 and a service crew on the field. Just as Sharp was leaving the

airport the air raid alarm sounded and he had to taice the DC-two off and
fly it away. It was a false alarm as the Japs raided a field between
Chungking and Wahsien but Sharp had to fly for two hours before he could
come back and land.
That afternoon about five both Sharp and Leonard went
to lancow and took f1fteen passengers each to Chengtu leaving Hanicow about
nine p.n. Everything went well except that both pilots ron into snow and
ice going over the mountains near Chengtu and both of them did not make
the time we hed hoped.
Sharp who was leading got out of Honkow on his
second trip just at day light but Leonard who was about twenty minutes
behind ran into an air raid over Hankon. He saw the planes but as no raid
warning hed been given him he thought they were Chinese until he sew the
bombs bursting on the airport.
then turned around and ran back to Ichang-
The air raid alarm service in
Hankow had been discontinued and evacuated.
After he got to Ichang I sent him word to return to Chungking. He was delayed
in getting gas at Ichang as we keep no gas on the field there, so he did not
get back to Chungking until after trelve noon.
He hed been flying almost
constantly since live ofclock the afternoon before and had flown to Hongkong
and back the night before that. I sent him home and told him his flighte for
that night were cancelled. He protested he was siright and would be able to
fly but Idid not listen to him.
When the raid, which Leonard just missed came over Hankow that
morning, all of Leonard's passengers were at the field waiting for the plane.
When the raid cane they scramed in all directions. Some hid in the drain
ditch around the rield, sone jumped into old bomb holes and some ducked into
a dug-out nearby. Mechanic Haynie who stopped to look atter the passengers
was the last men to make the dug-out and the Japs were machine-gunning him
not return. It took five hours to get him out and they had to back & car up
to the entrance.
The weather got worse until it becane clearly impossible to fly
over the mountains to Chengtu at night with any degree of safety at all, so
I wired Hankow we would have only one flight that night. The plane would
arrive just after dark and leave in the morning just at dawn for Chungking•
The replies we got to that from Hankow were really frantic.
I decided I
had better go down that night and explain our problems to the Minister.
Also I wanted to see Socony and I wanted to check up on the evacuation of our
staff.
The flight down was uneventful, the weather was bad and we flew
contact all the way. We had a bad icing condition with the temperature only
three degrees above freezing.
If we hed pulled up, as me would have to do
at night, it might have been difficuit. We got to Ichang and out of the
mountains just at dark and on into Honkow a little after eight.
The field
presented an eerie but interesting spectacle. It was a particularly dari
night and only small lanterns and flash lights were allowed. The field had
been heavily bonbed recently and none of the holes were being filled up.
All over the field were gangs of coolies digging and we were told they were
mining the field. I located the nearest bomb hole and made a mental note of
its bearing from the plane and I was all prepared to dive in it if necessary.

here were several olenes around. I recoznized a Junkers warming up an
a Beecherat't and 1 saw the Do-two wnion the Ministry of Communication
bought. Allison is flying it just now.
The Business Manager met me and told me he had nade an appoint-
ment for me to nee the Minister at ten that night. I went over to the
U.S.S. Luson and bed dinner and stayed until nearly ten when I went around
to the hotel to see the Minister. The Bund all along where the Luzon tied
up was crowded with Chinese soldiers but there was no semblance of order at
all. Many of them looked in the dark like convalescent wounded. There were
no guns or armed troupe nor was there any disorderly conduct that I saw.
Only hopeless confusion.
I saw the Minister and explained to him what the conditions were
and told him the next night if possible, we would fly two tripe each with
both DO-twos from Hankow to Ichang which was safer for the passengers and
then one trip each plane to Chungking. Also we would have two Commodores
out of Hankow for Ichang on the morning of the 25th. Also the Commodores
would return to Hankow from Ichang the evening of the 25th and would
evacuate the NAG staff on the morning of the 26th,
The Minister was very
much pleased, and said we were doing all that could be expected. General
Chen, Head of the Military Aviation was with the Minister and so was Ex-
Minister Chu Chia Hua.
I then went around to see the Secony people and got them out of
They said they expected to save all of our gas and eventusily get it
to Chungking. They also promised to send our gas up to Chungking on the
first trip their steamer nade which they thought would be soon, as soon
as the river got a little lower.
I then went around to NAC office and outlined all the evacuation
procedure for the morning of the 26th, Also I asiced our agent to give me all
the cash he had and I would take it back to Chungking with me. He bad about
thirty three thousend dollars in his safe. I took thirty thousand of it and
Left him the balance for emergency. I then went around to the Fienes Hotel
and got a room. It was then one ofclock in the morning and I had to get up
at three and I was so keyed up I never slept at all. I got up at three and
went back to CNAC*s office where the passengers were assembling.
They were
al there and they certainly were rearing to go. lie started out to the
field about four. The road out was thronged with people on foot evecusting.
Everything was ready and we got off about five just as it started to rain.
The trip back was also uneventful. The weather was the eaze as coning down
only it had got a little colder and we picked up a little ice but not much.
I learned while in Hankow that our Commodore did not get to Honkow that
afternoon but remained in Ichang. That upset me because every trip counted
and there was no reason for it not getting in.
On ny return to Chungking I bad breakfast and then went to the
office to work arranging the details for the flights that night and clearing
up some of the things on my desk.
I also sent a message to the pilot on the
Connodore who had remined in Ichang, Hugh Chen, telling him I would 11ke
for him to go on to lenkow that afternoon, the 24th, and fly back to Tehene
with passengers on the 25th, then return to Hankow on the evening of the 25th,

to evacuate the CHAd etaft on the morning of the 25th.
I sent the same
messege to the pilot on the other Commodore, loon Chinn, who was on he
I worked until two thirty without lunch
and then went to the airport to see Sharp and Leonard before they got
off at three forty five.
Everything was alright except the weather
which was bad as far as Ichang and not too good there.
Atter they left
I Left Nieh in charge and then I went home and went to bed at five in
the afternoon, Shortly after that I woke up and it was five thirty and
I wondered how it bad got dark so quickly. Then I realized I had slept
I slept again for another hour and then got up
and went to the airport.
I learned that Sherp and Leonard hed esch nade
one trip to Ichang and both had left Hankow agoin at day break.
Leonard
reported twenty passengers and Sherp nineteen. They were unable to make
two tripe to Ichung on account of the weather,
from Hankow to lengyang and return. I did not understand that. They both
Landed at Ichang and as the weather was getting worse and as Leonard wes
not tully emiliar with our Telefunken procedure at Chungking he reanined
at Ichang for the weather to improve but Sharp pulled up over the top and
çsme on in on the Telefunken. When he got bere I asked him about his
Hengyang trip and he told me he had flown the Generaliasino and the Madame
and W. H. Donald and several others down there. Pilot Just was supposed
to Ply them but Just who had never been to Fengyang objected to landing
there at night.
They arranged for Allison to fly them down in the DO-two
the Miniatry of Conmuniestions hed bought. Allison got out about half an
hour and his radio and lights went out so he had to return to Hankow.
was there and Allison appealed to him so Sharp flew then down with Allison as his
ao-pilot. Sharp said the Madone seemed very pleased and when they landed at
Hengyang she thonked him for herself and the Generaliasino for his aid. It
was a good break for NAC and Sharp used his bead.
Sharp also told me that when be got to Ichang he discovered he had
twenty passengers and not nineteen.
Just as he started to taxi away some
Chinese ran and opened the door of the plane and climbed in. We had no
ateward and no one reported him. Leonard had twenty two passengers, wo
climbed in on him.
Checking up on the Commodores I found that both of them bed left
Hankow at day bresk, one with staff.
I also had a message from H. Chen
saying he was proceeding to Chungking as there were only eleven of the
staff left and Moon Chinn would go back for them. Chinn went back that
afternoon as scheduled and landed about fifteen minutes before dark.
The
city on both sides of the river was on fire and Japanese were reported to be
entering the city on the North. There were only two of our coolies at the
poontoon waiting, who told him the nechanies had decided no one wus coming
back for them so
they got in our old Ford station wagon, bought as a second-
hand car before I arrived in Chine in March, 1951, and started for Ichang•
The two coolies got left so they decided to return
to the water front
hoping a plane would return. The situation was getting so hot Chian was
atraid to wait until morning and as there was no reason for him to do so,
ne took oil just at dark and flew to Shaai and landed there at night on the
river with no lighta. It was his firet night Plight. He came in in a long

note - Please
excuse this narrative but I had to write it
WLB

flat power glide with his co-pilot hanging out of the window watching the
; river and loon peering ahend for sempans or junks. When they seemed to
be about eight or ten feet off the water the co-pilot yelled and Moon
pulled back on his throttles and eased back on his stick and shut his eyes
and prayed to Buddha.
The next morning he took off for Ichang where he
Landed and filled up
his plane with passengers we had left there and returned
to Chungking•
it is over.
no one could keep that up long• I don't see how they accomplished as much as
2 or no arcade ty or 1r hang but
they did. I think the Minister van plessed.
I would like to say that Allison also flew to Hankow every night
The firet night there was nothing for him to do so he
returned to Chungking at day break bringing some of NAC's staff, a lot of
meil and pay passengers for CA. The second night, he brought gone aviation
and other officiols and mall for CNAC. The third night after his return
from Hengyang with Sharp, he brought fourteen pay passengers to Chungking for
CNAC after spending one night en route at Ichang.
He then told me be was
ordered to fly to Kunming on the 29th and would be glad to take passengers
but unfortunately his orders were chonged and he did not go to Kunming.
I don't know if you are still reading this or it you have
consigned it to the waste basket where it rightly belongs. I think we may say
that one period of the war is ending, and the tuture may be different.
certainiy looks bad for China now but actually it seems to me it is not waally
as bad as it was after the fall of Manking nearly a year ago.
Chinese are worse off but so are the Japanese, much worse off. They are
getting further from their base, apparently they are realling beginning to feel
the pinch, and they have no more big important towns or objectives they can
work towards with the feeling that if they can take that, their situstion will
Improve.
Alao the Japanese are undoubtedly beginning to
weaken thenselves at
home and they ere getting themselves into a very vulnerable position for sone
other nation to take advantage of. If the Chinese will juat hold on I believe
they have a good chance to get very favourable peace terms. I think the
Generaliasino will certainly keep up the fight.
It all depends on how China
unites behind him. I have been saying for a long time that we should Inow
something definite in sixty days.
Again I think we should. It may not be
good nows. It may be a bad pesce for China or it nay be the cortain knowledge
that China will keep on fighting to the bitter end but whatever the future has
In store should be developed in sixty daye I think.
It is not a very pleasant outlook but at lesst CNAC is still
fairly well organized and is7going concern with a little reserve. I think
CNAC will probabiy go back into the Red again before long but by doing a lot
of drastie reorganizing when it becomes necessary we will manage to hold on.
CHAC takes a lot of licking.
Yours very truly,
Copy Mr. Bixby

properties.sfomuseum:description: Typewritten letter from W.L. [William L.] Bond to S. [Stokely] W. Morgan, dated October 29, 1938, marked “Personal”; includes detailed description of CNAC’s efforts at the request of the Minister in the evacuation of Hankow [Hankou] by air; mentions [K.I.] Nieh, [Ernest] Allison, [Charles] Sharp, [Royal] Leonard, [Troy] Haynie, General Chen, ex-Minister Chu Chia Hua, “the Generalissimo” and “the Madame” [Chiang Kai-Shek and Madame Chiang], Moon [Fon] Chinn, Hugh Chen, [Eric] Just.
